name: creature
author: LLM, from a scenario. Note what it does NOT say: it never mentions legs.
scenario: A body that stands up under its own weight and stays standing when the ground shifts. It should hold itself clear of the ground rather than sprawl, survive a real tilt without toppling, and not be an implausible pile of matter. Nothing here asks for four legs — asking for legs would only rediscover my own assumption. Legs, if they appear, are the ANSWER.

constraints.why: THE GATE. The centre of gravity must project inside the support polygon. Otherwise it is not a creature, it is a thing lying down.

the tilt it can survive before toppling. This is the term that killed the LOLLIPOP: a boulder on a pole tips at 7.8 degrees, a quadruped at 26.6. It makes holding mass high COST you the robustness you need to keep it there — and the only way to buy both is to spread weight onto separated supports.
the body must be carried clear of the ground. Without this a pancake wins: perfectly stable, and useless.

REPAIR (2026-07-14), and the machine found the bug, not me. With only bounds, every constraint saturates at sat=1.0, the score pins at 1.0000, and there is NO GRADIENT LEFT TO CLIMB — the optimiser stops dead at 'barely legal'. The first run rode tip_deg=22.04 against its min of 22 and height=0.2212 against its min of 0.22, and produced a minimally-compliant blob on stilts. A spec made only of walls gets you exactly the walls. This term keeps paying past the wall.
the other half of the same repair: keep rewarding a body carried higher, not merely high enough.
a soft PRIOR, not a law. Real development is symmetric because it is cheap, not because symmetry is fit.
metabolic cost, charged by VOLUME not by bone count. Charging per bone was the other half of the lollipop: mass goes as r-squared, so one enormous bone was free.
an animal, not a stick figure and not a hairball.
